newsitem.title: GREECE: FEATURE - Bloody vendettas boom on Greek island of Crete.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Bloody vendettas boom on Greek island of Crete.

text.p: The pale, bedridden young man has done little but stare through the window at the swaying trees since he was shot seven years ago in a family vendetta, a resurgent old custom on the Greek island of Crete.

"I was ambushed by a whole family. They blocked the road with their car. The mother and daughter threw stones at me and the father took out a pistol and shot me in the neck," Yannis Strilingas, 31, told Reuters.

The death toll from the blood feud between branches of the Strilingas family that has left Yannis paralysed from the neck down numbers four dead, including both his parents. The man who shot him was his uncle, Charidimos Strilingas.
The vendetta, which forced the family to abandon its ancestral home of Livadia and come to this sprawling farm village near the town of Rethymno, is one of several to make headlines in recent years.
In 1988 Greek public opinion was stunned when an 80-year old father shot dead his son's killer as he was being tried for the murder in a crowded court.
"A 1995-1996 statistic showed Crete had one of the highest murder rates in Greece," said George Grammatikakis, former dean of the University of Crete, who has led a gun control campaign since 1990.
Crete is the last area of Greece where families engage in vendettas, an archaic custom fed by their love for weapons, strong sense of property and proverbial pride, he said.
A boom in illegal arms smuggling on the island in the past decade has rekindled vendettas, which also occur in Sicily and other Balkan countries, he added.

"There is one active vendetta spanning over 100 years with 40 to 50 dead and another that wiped out a whole village overnight in 1948," said social anthropologist Aris Tsantiropoulos, who is researching the issue for the University of the Aegean.

Vendettas usually start with an offence such as animal stealing or an accidental killing. The offended family must kill the adversary's senior heir in an effort to cut off the family line. The feud can go on until everyone is killed.
"A vendetta is catastrophe for the whole community. Most of the villagers have some relationship to the feuding families and they are obliged to take sides," Tsantiropoulos said.
Vendettas are more frequent in western Crete, in towns such as Sfakia and the villages of Milopotamos between the major towns of Iraklio and Rethymno.
In the old days a family could escape by moving away but now an avenger will travel far and wide to trace and kill his victim.
"With improved transport, we have vendetta murders as far as the island of Rhodes and the northern Greek town of Amaliada," Tsantiropoulos said.

The earliest written records of Cretan vendettas are 15th and 16th century documents left by the island's Venetian rulers. Western travellers also wrote in the 1800s that all the people in Sfakia wore black in a sign of mourning for vendetta victims in their families.
Tsantiropoulos believes the rise of deadly violence on Crete relates to the abrupt urbanising of their small, closed farming communities.
"These are not happy people. Their village-based, farming way of life has been changed drastically by outside forces. They can't cope," he said.

But Grammatikakis says the abundance of illegal firearms and the authorities' reluctance to tackle the problem are bound to cause more trouble. Law abiding people are under the constant psychological blackmail by those bearing arms.
Even the famous Cretan tradition of shooting in the air at weddings has got out of control, causing injuries and deaths.
"I get wedding invitations saying 'Please don't bring guns'. The custom was for the best man to fire an heirloom gun once, but now everyone wants to use machine-guns," he said.

He says modern, consumer-oriented Cretans interpret the old traditions wrongly -- the love for cherished old weapons left from father to son for generations has turned into a passion for machine guns and magnums as status symbols.

But not only the availability of guns has made vendettas resurface in recent years. Delays in Crete's judicial system have made people mistrust the law and eager to take things into their own hands, Grammatikakis said.

"When courts take up to 10 years to deliver a verdict it's no wonder people want personal vengance," he said. "If we improve our court system and make it faster it is sure to strike a blow at vendettas."
